qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

On 9 July 2026, Ann Widdecombe, a former British minister and former Member of the European Parliament, was murdered at her home having been struck 21 times with a hammer1. The investigation has been handed over to the counter-terrorism police, who have described the murder as a planned and targeted attack. The suspect who was arrested has been described by Nigel Farage as a left-wing extremist: ‘I have it on good authority that the murder suspect was a hard-Left activist. He attended various marches and hated anyone with an opposing view. He had expressed his hatred of me on more than one occasion. He was an intolerant individual obsessed with Soviet communism. He may also have been known to the authorities’2. As part of this investigation, the counter-terrorism police have also reopened an investigation into an attempted burglary and arson attack at a property linked to Nigel Farage. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this case and of the current status of the investigation into the murder of our former fellow Member of the European Parliament?
Do the Commission and its agencies, Europol and Eurojust, anticipate a wave of far-left terrorism, given the ongoing radicalisation of certain sections of our societies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.10.2026) As criminal investigations in the United Kingdom (UK) fall fully under the responsibility of the UK authorities, the Commission is not in a position to comment on the case. Any police or judicial cooperation in this matter at European level would take place between the competent UK authorities and the European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) and the European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation (Eurojust), strictly within the limits of their applicable Regulations1 and cooperation arrangements. The Commission continues to follow developments in terrorism and violent extremism of all ideological motivations through analytical work, such as Europol’s annual Terrorism Situation and Trend Report2, and assessments provided by the European Union Intelligence and Situation Centre. Assessments concerning possible trends, including far‑left terrorism, remain primarily the responsibility of Member States’ competent authorities and are carried out by Member States’ security services. Other tools at EU level, such as Eurojust’s Counterterrorism Register, facilitate judicial cooperation in this area. To further strengthen EU support to Member States, and as announced in ProtectEU: Internal Security Strategy3, the Commission has presented a comprehensive legislative package to reinforce the mandates of Europol and Eurojust to step up the fight against cross-border crime and terrorism.
